title: Gibbs free energy and feasibility; Rate equations and orders; Arrhenius equation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN07#t3 term and clue written for the game; KN07#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN07#t1 term and clue written for the game; EN09#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN09#N.5, KN04#N.3a, KN07#N.3, KN04#N.6a, KN07#N.12, KN07#N.13a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Catalyst
items.clue: Lowers Ea, so k is larger at the same temperature.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: Symbol Ea; a large value makes k more sensitive to temperature.

items.label: Rate constant
items.clue: The quantity k, fixed only at one temperature; it rises when T rises.

items.label: Gibbs energy
items.clue: The quantity ΔG; it is zero when T = ΔH/ΔS and says nothing about rate.

questions.stem: For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), calculate ΔG at 298 K. ΔH = −136 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −120.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Answers in kJ mol⁻¹.
The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². At constant temperature, the concentrations of A and B are both doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
questions.explanation: Doubling [A] gives ×2¹ = 2; doubling [B] gives ×2² = 4. The rate rises by 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.stem: For a reaction with Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K almost doubles the rate. Which statement gives the main reason for this large increase?

options.text: A much larger fraction of all the collisions now have energy equal to or greater than Ea.
The particles move faster, so they collide more often, and more collisions give more reactions.
The activation energy decreases as the temperature rises, so more of the collisions succeed.
Every particle gains the same amount of energy, which carries many more of them past Ea.

questions.stem: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?

options.text: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, as the rate constant has the same units as the rate
mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, as k = rate/[A]² for a second-order reaction
s⁻¹, as only one reactant, A, appears in the rate equation
mol³ dm⁻⁹ s⁻¹, as k = rate × [A]² when the rate equation is rearranged

questions.explanation: (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, for any reaction that is second order overall.

questions.stem: Reactions 1 and 2 have the same Arrhenius factor, A. Reaction 1 has the larger activation energy. Both are plotted as ln k against 1/T on the same axes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Reaction 1's line is less steep, as a larger Ea makes k less sensitive to temperature.
The lines are parallel, with reaction 1's line lower, as Ea only shifts the line down.
Reaction 1's line has a positive gradient, as its k rises faster with temperature.
Reaction 1's line is steeper, and both lines meet the ln k axis at one point.

questions.explanation: Larger Ea, steeper line. Intercept = ln A, the same for both.

questions.stem: A clock reaction is timed at several temperatures, with the same starting concentrations each time. Rate ∝ 1/t, so ln(1/t) stands in for ln k. On a plot of ln(1/t) against 1/T / 10⁻³ K⁻¹, two points on the line are (3.10, −2.30) and (3.40, −4.25). What is Ea? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
